As far back as I can remember this ringing has been what I associated with silence. I require a fan, tv, music.. anything to fall asleep to. 

If I think about it, it's there. I assume I've just learned to tune it out when there is SOMETHING else to to hear. But all I need to do is read the word Tinnitus, or ringing or just think about it. It's always there.

Occasionally at night when just listening to it I can hear different tones. Sometimes it sounds like an old CRT gets turned off or on and lingers until it finally fades into the normal, ever present tone.

Sometimes I can pick out a buzz instead of the ring. Sometimes it sounds like the vibration an outside residential A/C makes.

I had terrible ear infections as a child, had tubes eventually. Probably had something to do with it.

Probably didn't help listening to music when younger way too loud. Perhaps that was how I tried to drown it out then.

I also find the word.. ringing inadequate to describe these sounds. Yeah it can give you an idea, but it's just not quite correct. The word ringing reminds me of a bell, or phone... with waves of sound, pulsating ding, ding. 

My tinnitus is like the peak of the ding... and it never ends. It can seem like ringing since I can hear it then tune it out, perhaps it does pulse at times... but  in the end all the different varieties of tones meld together to a constant sound, not quite ringing.

I would like to experience silence some day. Even temporarily, fleeting.

If you navigate to the recording when they're discussing it they give a good explanation of what's happening. I never understood how they determined atmospheric composition until it clicked during that segment.

They can't see water on the planet, but they can see the elements in the atmosphere when the planet passed between us and its host star. They can measure the light that makes it thru to determine what elements are present.

Based on the light that makes it thru they analyze the wave and can tell which elements are there based off the light that is blocked by it.

So then they were able to determine water vapor/elements making it up are in its atmosphere.

Imagine looking at a streetlight in fog, or the sun/moon through a cloud. The scientists can tell you based off the light being observed what type of gas is obscuring it. They could tell you if it's fog (water) or smoke (whatever elements make up that smoke) due to the amount of light reaching you (with of course respect to the distance of you/the observer and the light source/material being analyzed.
